paras: The assault on a Black minister in Oklahoma City was an attack in 1920 in which a white man insulted and assaulted a Black minister, after which the city's police court judge dismissed the case against him. It is known from an editorial in the Black Dispatch, "The Place Where Lynchers Are Born," which the New York Age summarized and quoted on August 14, 1920, as an example of lower courts encouraging mob violence.

According to the editorial, a white man whom it called "a white reprobate" insulted and assaulted "a most respectable black man, a minister of the gospel" in Oklahoma City. Neither the minister nor his assailant is named, and the coverage gives no date, place within the city, or description of injuries.

The case came before the judge of the Oklahoma City police court, who, in the Age's words, "washed his hands of" it and dismissed it. The editorial referred to a "Judge Munder" who would "applaud their brutality and dismiss their cases," a name that may be an epithet or an error in the text rather than the judge's own. No report of any further proceeding against the white man was found.

The Black Dispatch used the dismissal to argue that police courts were "the shambles in which the mob and the jellish lyncher is born." Its editor wrote that lynchers began as "white boys on the street" who insulted Black men and women, carried guns, kept a gang nearby, and expected lenient judges, and that lynching would end only when such men knew they would be "hunted down and meted out justice."

The New York Age carried the editorial in a column of comment from other Black papers and added that the South, "as well as Oklahoma," needed a uniform administration of justice in the lower courts and among sheriffs and police. No account of the assault or the hearing was found in the white press, and the original Black Dispatch editorial was not located.

accounts.label: Black Dispatch editorial (via New York Age)
accounts.gist: A white man insulted and assaulted a respectable Black minister, and the Oklahoma City police court judge dismissed the case; the editor argued that such leniency toward white street toughs is where lynch mobs are bred.

framing.detail: The Black Dispatch headed its editorial 'The Place Where Lynchers Are Born' and called the police court 'the shambles in which the mob and the jellish lyncher is born'; the New York Age reprinted it with a call for uniform justice in the lower courts.
